newsitem.title: REPUBLIC OF IRELAND: Jubilant Sinn Fein in Irish election launch.
newsitem.headline: Jubilant Sinn Fein in Irish election launch.

text.p: Bolstered by record scores in two British elections, the IRA's political wing Sinn Fein enters Ireland's June 6 parliamentary poll on Monday seeking to build its case for inclusion in Northern Ireland peace talks.

Sinn Fein President Gerry Adams will launch the party's manifesto and seek to bring the same dramatic improvement in the party's showing in Ireland that brought it a record 17 per cent of votes in local elections in British-ruled Northern Ireland last week.
That vote capped its take in Britain's May 1 elections, which saw Ssinn Fein's support rise to 16 per cent and elected Adams and his chief lieutenant Martin McGuinness to the British parliament.
Sinn Fein, which wants to end British rule of Northern Ireland and reunite it with the Irish republic, scores around two per cent of votes in Irish elections and has no members of parliament.
But it believes that support for its demand for automatic inclusion in the Northern Ireland peace talks could garner the same kind of improved backing it received north of the border.
Britain says that only an unconditional end to violence by its Irish Republican Army (IRA) guerrilla allies will grant it the right to join pro-British Unionists at the peace talks.

Its manifesto launch takes place weeks after Irish Prime Minister John Bruton advised Northern Ireland's electorate that a vote for Sinn Fein was a vote for continued IRA violence and prolonging a 28-year conflict that has killed 3,200.

But Sinn Fein, which has lived on the fringes of mainstream politics for decades, says it is a legitimate political party distinct from the IRA and should be at the peace talks by virtue of its electoral mandate.
Last week British officials met Sinn Fein negotiators for the first time since the IRA ended a 17-month truce and killed two people with a London bomb that led to international isolation.

Irish officials have also dropped a ban on contact at civil servant level and U.S. President Bill Clinton is expected to tell Sin Fein to build on the openings to secure a new IRA ceasefire when he visits London this week.

Few give Sinn Fein a chance of winning a seat in the poll, which pits the centre-left coalition of Bruton against the confident opposition alliance of Bertie Ahern's Fianna Fail and Mary Harney's Progressive Democrats.

But opinion polls are pointing to a hung parliament being returned, which could give the party leverage if it manages to capture a seat in the traditionally Irish republican strongholds along the border or in southern Kerry county.
The latest, in Dublin's Sunday Independent newspaper, said Bruton's so-called Rainbow Coalition with the leftist Labour Party and Democratic Left is making a comeback.

The IMS poll, taken last Thursday, showed the coalition would win 42 per cent of votes, an increase of two per cent over the previous poll earlier in May, and the Fianna Fail and Progressive Democrat grouping would win 45 per cent.

But given a straight choice 46 per cent would prefer Fianna Fail's Ahern as the next Prime Minister while 39 per cent would opt for Bruton, who came to power when the previous Fianna Fail-led government collapsed at the end of 1994.
